speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It instituted the rights of women, and protected vulnerable women and girls exposed to vice.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The Women's Charter was also pivotal in strengthening the family institution, which is a key pillar of our society.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It upheld monogamy and outlined the rights and duties of married persons.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Strong marriages and families are as important and relevant today, if not more so.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: However, with the passage of time, families evolve.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And families in Singapore are changing as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: First, there are more dual-income families where both the husband and wife work.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We also see small, but increasing instances, of wives being the main breadwinner.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Second, divorces are becoming more common among recent cohorts, especially so for couples who got married at a very young age.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Children are often adversely affected, even long after the divorces.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The vast majority are genuine but there are also some marriages of convenience for immigration advantage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Fourth, the increasing prevalence of social media, which requires new measures to protect those who experience family violence and also the professionals who engage in protection work.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Our social policies, infrastructure and legal provisions must be regularly updated to support families.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The proposed legislative amendments we are making to the Women's Charter today are one part of this larger effort.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: First, we must continue to strengthen marriages and families.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is, and will remain, one of the Ministry of Social and Family Development's (MSF's) key priorities.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have different services, programmes and public outreach initiatives towards this objective.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: However, notwithstanding these efforts, divorces are becoming more common.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Marriages involving couples where one or both parties are very young face a higher risk.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: A fair number are not adequately prepared for marriage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Those who become parents shortly after marriage do face additional stress.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In 2011, the Women's Charter was amended to require minor couples to attend a Marriage Preparation Programme if one party is below the age of 18, or if both parties are minors below 21.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: About 200 minor couples have gone through the programme.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Agencies that currently conduct the Marriage Preparation Programme will do so for this additional group of couples.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This will take effect for marriages on and after 1 October 2016.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Beyond legislation, we will also enhance the pre- and post-marriage support continuum for this group of couples.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will put in place group marriage education programmes, one-on-one marriage assessments and post-marriage support sessions by 2017.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Even as we try to strengthen marriages, there will be those that have irretrievably broken down.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Divorcing couples and their family members go through periods of anger, anxiety, grief and stress.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The children are often the ones most adversely impacted when caught in the middle of their parents' fights.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: There was a child whose paternal grandmother told her that if she really loved her daddy, she should stop thinking of mommy.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The little girl grieved over this but hid it from her dad and grandmother because she did not want to disappoint them; she did not want to make them angry.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: There was a child who was told by her mother that her daddy did not love her anymore, as he had a new family with a new baby.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: She asked whether her mommy would also not love her anymore if she had a new baby herself.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: These are stories which the children shared with some of our workers who work with families.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And these stories tell us that we must always make sure that children's voices are heard and their interests and needs are taken care of during divorces.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In 2011, the Ministry amended the Women's Charter to require divorcing parents with children to attend mandatory mediation and counselling after a writ of divorce has been filed.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This has been quite effective in helping some divorcing couples to reach agreements on children's matters in less acrimonious ways.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But going for mandatory mediation and counselling on children's issues, after first battling it out in Court to settle the divorce, is really not ideal.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Many divorcing parties have become hardened Page: 36 in their positions or too caught up with their emotions by then.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The new pre-divorce MPP will cover a range of issues that will have a tangible impact on children such as housing, school, care arrangements, and bread and butter.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: These practical aspects, when overlooked, add unnecessary turmoil to a child's life post-divorce.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The new mandatory programme will also stress the importance of positive co-parenting after divorce.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Even though a marriage ends, parental responsibilities remain.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And it is important that parents remember that.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Children need both parents to co-parent even after divorce.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Allow me to say this with the best of intentions.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But, in many cases, it is probably the best "gift" that divorced parents can give to their children – the certainty that they still have both parents to love them despite everything.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Then, the children do not feel that they have to take sides; they do not feel they are to blame; and they do not feel guilty.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The process which divorcing parents go through in applying for MPP will also include self-reflection questions − questions that focus parents' minds on their children's well-being.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: For those who may still have questions about their marriage and divorce, we will also point them to agencies that provide marital counselling.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I hope that with this, perhaps some, upon reflection, may actually reconsider divorce and seek help for their problems.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: During our public consultation on the Bill, some members of the public expressed concern that the new mandatory requirement could lengthen the divorce process.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They felt that in some situations, for example, where there is family violence, the divorce process needs to be expeditious.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Neither do we aim to make it easier.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But the objective is to better equip parties with knowledge and awareness of the issues arising in a divorce that will affect their children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It will enable couples to be more informed and make child-centric decisions during the process of divorce.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: These four agencies offer a range of programmes and services.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The feedback from the couples and their children, as well as from judges and community partners, has been positive.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I will now move on to the next area of amendments, which is on maintenance.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Today, under the Women's Charter, maintenance may be ordered for two broad categories.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Both fathers and mothers are responsible for maintaining or contributing to the maintenance of their children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is so even after a divorce, whether or not they have custody of the children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: A mother may, therefore, seek child-maintenance from the father, and vice Page: 37 versa.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The second category of maintenance is for a spouse or ex-spouse.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is the focus of the proposed amendment.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Today, a woman can seek spousal maintenance from her husband or ex-husband.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The law, however, does not enable men to seek spousal maintenance from their wives or ex-wives.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is something that is increasingly being questioned and debated, and my Ministry has certainly received a broad range of opinions.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: At one end of the spectrum, some Singaporeans have argued that spousal maintenance should be gender-blind and based on needs.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The writer wrote, "I find it hard to believe that Singapore, a First World society, is unable to accept that women should be our equals and should provide towards maintaining their ex-spouse equally if he is unable to do so." Along this line of argument, some Singaporeans proposed that matters relating to marriage and divorce be addressed through a new "Family Charter", rather than the Woman's Charter.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: At the other end of the spectrum, there are those who feel strongly that men should be the main breadwinner – and by and large, they remain so – and spousal maintenance should be reserved for women only.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: After all, a wife is more likely to give up her career to care for the family.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: She is also more likely to be financially more vulnerable post-divorce.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Allow me to quote from two emails we have received to illustrate.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: One said, "Despite the call of gender equality, we must face the reality that there cannot be absolute equality between the two genders.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Moreover, it remains in our culture and, in fact, among men themselves, the notion that the husband is deemed the "protector" of the family." Another argued: "Remember that the Women's Charter is supposed to protect women's rights and not allow women to fall prey to the irresponsibility of men who wilfully refused to work, in the name of providing care for the family." Clearly, there are very emotive and strong responses from various ends of the spectrum and in between them as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I do not honestly think there is one decision that can satisfy all the differing views.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is one issue where there will be a range of issues.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Indeed, there are more women today with more successful careers.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Some of you may have read about a recent Court of Appeal judgment which disallowed a woman's claim for a nominal maintenance order of $1.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The Court found her "more than capable" of taking care of herself.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: On the other hand, we still have many women who are struggling to provide a decent home for herself and her children, after years of being a homemaker during the marriage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As Members of Parliament, I think many of us would have encountered such real-life examples during our Meet-the-People Sessions and when we meet our residents.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: There remain many vulnerable women, and many women who hold rank-and-file jobs who need to be able to rely on their husbands or ex-husbands for maintenance for themselves and their children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: However, we do note the feedback provided and we will keep this issue on watch and Page: 38 consider it in the future.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That said, we do feel that time is right for us to take a step to allow incapacitated husband and ex-husbands to apply for spousal maintenance where there is a clear need.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Recently, one of our divorce support specialist agencies highlighted a case they handled.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This concerns a man with a professional job.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: He was unfortunately struck with a debilitating illness while on an overseas work assignment.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The illness left him mentally incapacitated and unable to work.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: His wife, equally successful in her career, divorced him and now he has no way to support himself.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In yet another case, my Parliamentary Secretary met a male resident who became severely disabled after a serious work accident.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is part and parcel of the mutual help and support expected when a man and a woman enter into a marriage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Stories, such as what I have shared, reinforce our sense that this is one area in which we should do more.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have set three clear criteria that must all be met.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: He must also be unable to support himself at the time when the maintenance application is heard.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: For clarity, I will give some examples which will not be covered.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: These include: (a) an incapacitated husband or ex-husband who is able to earn a livelihood sufficient to maintain himself; (b) an incapacitated husband or ex-husband who has other means, such as income from investments or insurance pay-outs, to support himself; and (c) an ex-husband who became incapacitated after the divorce has been finalised.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: An ex-wife is not expected and does not have any obligation to provide spousal maintenance if her ex-husband does not meet the criteria up to the point of divorce.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: During our public consultation, we also received a lot of feedback on maintenance enforcement.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I think many of us feel very strongly about this issue; I certainly do.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have received many heartfelt appeals and letters talking of maintenance payments slipping, being irregular or not being paid.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I can understand how frustrating this can be for an ex-spouse who is not only entitled to but also relies on the maintenance to keep the family going after divorce.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In the last round of amendments in 2011, we introduced several measures to strengthen maintenance enforcement.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Today, the Court may order a defaulter's employer to pay maintenance directly out of the defaulter's salary, mandate that a defaulter attend financial counselling and even sentence a defaulter to jail.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Page: 39 We do not need more legislative changes this round on this front.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Many of the challenges lie instead with implementation.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is where we need to improve and this is what we must tackle.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: To this end, my Ministry has been working closely with the Family Justice Courts and the Community Justice Centre to strengthen the working relationship among our agencies.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: For example, he could be in jail or has had a serious accident and cannot work.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Such wives or ex-wives will be directed to my Ministry's Social Service Offices (SSOs) for financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Our SSOs will also refer them to the Community Justice Centre for legal assistance should there be a need.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Our focus here is on the women and children, as they are often the victims.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But that said, we will also help a husband or ex-husband whose circumstances have changed such that he genuinely cannot pay maintenance.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: For example, if he has a serious debilitating illness and is not able to work for a sustained period, he may approach the Community Justice Centre for legal assistance to review the maintenance orders.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The SSOs will help not only the man, but also his wife or ex-wife, with financial assistance so that the family may tide over the difficult period and get back on their feet.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In contrast to this more empathetic approach, we do intend to be very much more firm with these recalcitrant maintenance defaulters in the so-called "won't pay" group this means those who have the means but choose not to honour their maintenance payments.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is where there is much distress, anger and bitterness on the part of wives and ex-wives especially.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This officer will assist the Court in certain maintenance enforcement applications so as to identify those who can afford but refuse to pay maintenance.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: With the assessment of the individual's ability to pay, judges will be in a better position to make full use of the range of enforcement levers introduced in the 2011 round of amendments.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Judges can impose tougher penalties against these recalcitrant individuals and I hope that they do.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As Members, and many of you can relate to this, we have encountered many heartrending appeals from divorced parents to see their children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Often, it is the fathers who have been denied access.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: With an increase in capacity, our agencies will be better able to facilitate child access arrangements.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Very importantly, they will work with parents to co-parent more effectively.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As a husband and a father, I would like to take this opportunity to remind all men to be responsible, especially when you have child maintenance to pay.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Parenting your child does not stop even when the marriage is over.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: You can still and always be a loving father by not neglecting your responsibility to provide for your children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Even if your marriage is over, a caring relationship with you as a father will help your child to heal and learn to trust all over again.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: So, not only in terms of maintenance, spend time.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Earlier, I mentioned that there are more marriages between Singaporeans and non-Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The vast majority of such marriages are genuine.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But there are instances where parties enter into a sham marriage for immigration purposes.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In 2012, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) introduced a provision in the Immigration Act criminalising such marriages for immigration advantage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Parties convicted can be fined or imprisoned, or both, with their immigration facilities revoked.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is an offence for parties to abuse marriage laws for immigration advantage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It follows, therefore, that such marriages should be void.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The new section 11A will now make a marriage void if one party to the marriage is convicted of the marriage of convenience offence under the Immigration Act.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Men, women and children who experience family violence require help.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Today, in the event of violence within the family, a married man or woman below 21 years of age has to rely on others, such as a parent or a guardian, to apply for a protection order on his or her behalf.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Given that most married persons below 21 years old already have familial responsibilities, such as care of children, section 65 is to be amended to provide for married or previously married persons below 21 years old to apply for protection orders for themselves and their children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is similar to the provisions in the Act that govern the parties allowed to apply for maintenance orders.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Some women and girls in crisis situations may, at times, need temporary emergency accommodation at places of safety, such as crisis shelters or residential facilities.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The Bill introduces new community-based care options by allowing the Director of Social Welfare to also place a vulnerable woman or girl below 21 years of age into the care of a "fit individual".

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This could be a relative or friend who could provide support in a "home environment", and not only in residential facilities or shelters.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Some professionals that my Ministry works with in protection work include the staff in Family Service Centres, Family Violence Specialist Centres and crisis shelters.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will provide immunity for such professionals when they assist vulnerable individuals or discharge their duties in good faith and with reasonable care.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In this way, they are protected against lawsuits or other legal proceedings in their personal capacity when carrying out a Court order, acting under the direction of the Minister or the Director of Social Welfare in discharging duties under the Act.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The rise of online platforms and social media poses new dangers to victims of abuse and also challenges to the professionals who protect them.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: A new section 177A will prohibit the publication or broadcast of any information in the mass and social media that would reveal or is likely to identify the location of the shelter, residential facility or its residents.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is to better prevent perpetrators of violence from harassing, intimidating or harming persons residing or working at places of safety.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The state may also act against serious breaches by the media which compromise the safety of the residents and staff.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: A related amendment is made to section 153 to prohibit publishing of information via online media which may lead to women and girls being identified in certain in-camera Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The rise of online media has also allowed vice syndicates to take their businesses online to widen their reach to clients, while hiding behind the anonymity of the Internet.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This makes it challenging for the Police to prevent and detect criminal groups conducting such a business.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Page: 41 Sexual services at hotels and residences arranged by vice syndicates using new technologies also affect the public's sense of safety and security.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The family remains the key pillar of our society.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As families continue to change in Singapore, we will also have to continue to review our policies, services and programmes.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The legislative amendments I am proposing to the Women's Charter today are one part of this broad effort.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Many Singaporean organisations and individuals have contributed to this exercise.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Some have generously provided their professional knowledge and expertise.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Regardless of how far we have come, how much further we should go, one thing is for sure – as a nation, we pledged to build an equal and democratic society.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Prejudice against either gender is frowned upon in the workplaces and public domains.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, it is common to find that cultural baggage from the past continues to hinder our progress in the pursuit of gender equality.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This continues to be presumed and desired as the default relationship dynamic.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Husbands are expected to build their careers and bring home the bread, while the wives handle the kids and household matters, regardless of their interests and professional abilities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Women's Charter was established in 1961 to empower the law to protect women who were seen as the weaker sex.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Back in those days, many women did not pursue higher levels of learning and they would marry and become stay-home moms almost after leaving school.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Or they would quit their jobs when they decided to have a family.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Granting maintenance to women in a divorce has been the rightful thing to do in appreciation of her contribution to the family when she has sacrificed her youth and potential incomes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Page: 42 Many also held positions of authority in their workplaces.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: MSF has, for years, called for the extension of spousal maintenance to men.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, with this Bill, I would say any progress is good progress.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is good that we have made this small step.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I strongly believe that men who quit their jobs to become house-husbands on mutual consent and perform their designated roles adequately should also be entitled to maintenance.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Please note "mutual consent" because I also have residents who told me that their husbands are lazy to work and, hence, they are forced to become the sole breadwinner and some of them have to work day and night, taking on more than one job, and their husband goes out jalan-jalan.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, for cases like this, when it comes to divorce, the husband should not be entitled to any maintenance, even though he is not fit to work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The wife in this case earned slightly more than the husband, grossing $215,900 in annual income.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She also had more than twice the assets he had.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Justice Choo had rightly said that to award the woman even a token sum "would be wrong if it was merely symbolic.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: That symbol for women has to be torn asunder, in fact and in spirit".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is unfortunate that not every man in a similar situation gets a fair resolution.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have heard from divorce lawyers' cases where men have clearly been taken advantage of, though there is not much publicity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: More resources and enforcement should, in fact, be dedicated to spouses who are truly deserving of maintenance and alimony.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have to find a more effective means of prosecuting ex-spouses who default on maintenance fees that they are rightfully supposed to provide.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have encountered cases in which the women had to spend a lot of time frantically trying to secure much-needed child and financial support from their irresponsible ex-husbands.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Sometimes, a woman has to go to Court every few months to get her ex-husband to pay up.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In one of those cases, a woman had her case dragged on for 10 years and heard by over 20 judges.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She had given up her career for the sake of their four children and, upon divorce, was left to raise them on her own without monetary contribution from her ex-husband.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Imprisoning the man for a token few days as a punishment is hardly beneficial if he is determined to make the life of his ex-wife very difficult.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think a woman should not have to haul her husband off to Court repeatedly if he is habitually paying maintenance fees late or not paying up at all.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: His poor track record should be more than enough for immediate tougher action.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Right now, it is by definition the men who are defaulting.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But in the future, we could see women defaulting as well.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Reforms in this aspect will benefit spouses who are awarded alimony, whether male or female.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Page: 43 In 2014, Home Affairs and Law Minister K Shanmugam shared his concerns.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He said that a faster, simpler and more effective system is being planned to get defaulters to pay up.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to an update about this new system.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The process of seeking maintenance from an unwilling hand is, undoubtedly a gruelling and worrisome one.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope more support can be given to those long-suffering spouses.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There should also be pro bono lawyers to help with the legal matters.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There should be readily accessible support networks that they can tap on, with counsellors who can offer guidance and help to find fuss-free assistance for a range of related issues from financial aid to housing, health and school matters.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A marriage may not be salvageable, but both parents can, and should continue to conduct their parental responsibilities, assist their children to adapt to the changes, and possibly continue to carry significant responsibility in the later part of the children's lives.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Here is where I want to touch on visitation rights to children.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is something that needs to be addressed in the parenting programme as part of a post-divorce plan where all the arrangements concerning the child are mapped out, from visitation schedules, decision- making to parenting responsibilities and more.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, make counselling and support programmes for children of divorced marriages comprehensive and easily accessible.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Counsellors must work closely with parents to ensure that the children are attending the sessions and programmes as regularly as required with the goal of adapting well to their new life with one parent.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To conclude, we cannot prevent divorces, or the hard feelings that some divorces will bring.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But we need to minimise the adverse effects of divorces to our society, especially the children.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: An equal maintenance regime, where ex-spouses can easily seek arrears, and encouragement to cooperate on childcare are all factors that bring about this positive change.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   The amendments have two changes which can help families that, unfortunately, are going through divorce.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Today, there are many women who are as successful as men in the workplace.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, we can gradually move towards gender equality in terms of paying maintenance.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Minister for Law said before that the Ministry was studying some changes in this area.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the authorities can simplify the relevant procedures and give these women greater help.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On strengthening maintenance, enforcement and support, I agree with what the Minister has shared that it is not about increasing legislation and that we should consider the efficacy of the Page: 44 processes which are supposed to deliver the objectives espoused in the Women's Charter.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is especially relevant for those who face financial difficulty in the first place and can ill afford to take leave from work or from taking care of their children to go to the Family Courts to make the application in person and attend Court for the subsequent mentions or for the trials.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And in the case of "incapacitated husbands", I am not sure if he is physically able to make the application at the Family Courts should his ex-wife default.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Further, should the defaulter fail to turn up in Court, he or she can be found in contempt of the Court and a warrant of arrest issued.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, what in reality happens is that no arrest is actually made as warrants of arrests are issued for a variety of reasons including non-payment of parking fines or service and conservancy charges and it is impossible to task the Police to arrest every person who has a warrant of arrest issued against him or her.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, though a garnishee order can be made to secure maintenance payments against bank accounts, each garnishee order is once off, meaning, that the aggrieved party typically bundles months of arrears owed to him or her, before making an application for a garnishee order to the Courts and in the meantime, the aggrieved party faces financial difficulties without the maintenance payments.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are also instances where the bank account is closed by the defaulter and there is no information on his other bank accounts.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With that, I support the amendments to the Bill.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I would like to comment and seek clarification on some issues.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: On maintenance for incapacitated husbands, whilst I consider it as a right and humane thing to do, there are some who argue that we are drifting towards the equal rights issue where, in the past, such responsibility rested solely on the men with the traditional role of men supporting women Page: 45 instead of vice versa.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Some have also asked if this is going to be the beginning of change towards equal rights with more amendments to come on the Women's Charter to equalise in all aspects.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I can understand this argument because with our Asian values-based society here, we have yet to reach the level of gender equality to be looking at equal rights in all aspects.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, women are still under-represented at senior management levels; child-rearing and care-giving responsibilities are still considered roles for women with many young women having to put their jobs on hold; and also, some women are not paid equally as their male counterparts for similar jobs and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Another issue with this amendment, Madam, is the resultant burden being too excessive for some, if not all, of the divorced wives with incapacitated spouses.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This would be especially so for those with young children.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It will definitely be doubly difficult for a wife to look after the children and also the long-term needs of the incapacitated ex-husband.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In the past, the siblings or even the parents will take care of or share the care of the incapacitated spouses.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: With this Bill, this past norm of the extended family's responsibility will be shifted to the ex-wife and thus the possibility of leaving the entire long-term care to her.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Another point is that the extra long-term burden on the wife may indeed disadvantage her in getting into another relationship.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is because the potential new partner may not be comfortable with having his future wife supporting another person permanently.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Putting the child's interest first in a divorce through an MPP for divorcing parents with children below 21 years old is welcome, indeed.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Children do suffer from broken marriages through no fault of theirs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Studies have shown that children suffer from physical and psychological repercussions from the divorce of their parents.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Such children are at a higher risk of social and psychological problems later in their adult lives.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Studies have also shown that children whose parents are married throughout the early childhood years are less likely to suffer from breathing problems, such as asthma, from becoming overweight and from being injured in accidents before they are five years of age.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: On the other hand, children troubled with parental divorce are particularly prone to develop problems with anger, disobedience, rule violations, prolonged sadness and even depression.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Their performance in school can be adversely affected, too.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The emotional, social, health and economic costs associated with marital conflict and family dissolution causing delinquency, depression, poverty and crime and, especially, the devastating harm done to children, have been well-documented.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Most children are stressed and do not want their parents to divorce.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: According to studies by Amato and Keith in 1991, the long-term consequences of parental divorce for adult attainment and quality of life may prove to be more serious than the transitional short-term emotional and social problems in children.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Stress states have been noted to be prolonged for many children, especially those in lower-income families with financial instability following the divorce of their parents.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many children also have difficulty adjusting to new environments and perhaps new step-parents and step-siblings from any subsequent marriages.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I feel that this will be an important step to ensure keeping these children on MSF's radar in order to give them a better footing in life subsequently and thereby prevent future problems for themselves and for society.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Concerning the new section 94A of the Bill on extending the Mandatory Marriage Preparation Programme to marriages where at least one party is a minor, I read it as MSF trying to apply the tenet of "prevention is better than cure".

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is a good thing as divorces here are on the rise.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: MSF had previously published that marriages involving younger grooms, regardless of the age of the brides, were particularly vulnerable to divorces.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, this Mandatory Marriage Preparation Programme may be useful in preventing divorces.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I feel that we should particularly take the opportunity at this early stage to identify couples with high divorce potential and counsel them accordingly.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Over the past two decades, the US government-funded researchers have declared that they can predict, with about 90% accuracy, which engaged couples will divorce.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: An early researcher in the field, regarded by many as its reigning genius, is John Gottman.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Other researchers have developed programmes that can significantly change the odds for marriages that appear doomed.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Can MSF also set up a fund to make it easier for couples to have such courses without monetary constraints?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Regarding section 57C, I agree that we should strengthen our regulations to avoid marriages of convenience.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In our small country with limited resources, we cannot afford to allow this immigration loophole.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: When certain characteristics or signs, such as wide age gap, foreign bride and lower income, of a marriage of convenience exist, there should be extra measures in place to determine such applications.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Very often, conflicting answers to the same questions posed to such couples can give clues to such marriages of convenience.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could MSF facilitate better collaboration of the various Ministries involved in order to enhance higher vigilance and detection?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Can the registrars or, for that matter, any other Ministries refer with ease any suspected cases of marriage of convenience to MSF or the Immigration and Checkpoints Page: 47 Authority (ICA) for follow-up?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Most times, it is the public or people in the community that is in the know about any marriages of convenience between couples.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, we should try to make it easier and convenient for the public to inform on such couples so that the relevant Ministries can follow up.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope MSF can further facilitate these areas.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I also feel that publicity on our rules and punishments concerning marriages of convenience can be made clearer.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This should especially target the nationals that frequently use this route to gain permanent residency here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When enacted in 1961, the Women's Charter was a momentous and courageous legislation that swam against the tide of opinions and the traditional values of society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The preservation of the so-called traditional family was not the original intent of the Charter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the contrary, the Women's Charter instituted the modern moral view of the family as a cooperative partnership between husband and wife who have equal rights as independent individuals and have equal responsibilities in caring and providing for the children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a waste that the present and recent amendments are cautious reactions to rising divorce rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These were opportunities to replicate the visionary spirit of the framers of the original Charter in using the law to shape society for the empowerment of its members.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The main changes proposed by the present Bill attempt to deal with two sets of problems besetting the modern family following the principles of the original Charter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first set concerns the better protection of the well-being and interests of children and follows the principle of parental responsibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The proposed changes, each on their own and on the whole, do not go far enough to plug the widening cracks and empower the modern family in increasingly trying times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the matter of parental responsibility and better protection of children, I would like to make four points.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My worry is that divorcing parents would go through the motion of attending the MPP.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To be effective, the MPP should be tailored to parenting in divorced situations targeting both custodial and non-custodial parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It should be integrated with mandatory mediation and counselling of divorcing parents at the Child Focused Resolution Centre (CFRC) and should stretch across the pre-divorce and post-divorce periods.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, the MPP and the counselling should try to involve the children as much as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Children should not be treated simply as passive victims whose problems could be solved by positive parenting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Article 12 of the Convention of the Rights of the Child states that we should "assure to the child who is capable of forming his or her own views the right to express Page: 48 those views freely in all matters affecting the child" and that these views be "given due weight in accordance with the age and maturity of the child".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In divorcing situations, children should be and could be active stakeholders whose participation in the process could help to protect their interests and help them achieve some emotional closure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second point I would like to raise is that while parental courses, mediation and counselling are good soft solutions persuading couples to go through amicable divorce in the interest of their children, they do not solve the hard problem of ex-husbands defaulting on maintenance support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means thousands of children remain at serious financial risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Repeated stalling and refusal to pay maintenance could be the continuation of abusive relationships, specifically economic abuse to deprive other members of the family the sustenance to maintain a decent standard of living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Charter continues to fail to recognise this as a form of family violence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even if we allow that most ex-husbands who default on maintenance simply failed to put responsibility to their children as a priority in their economic affairs, this goes against the Charter's core principle of equal parental responsibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whatever it is, the children suffer and may grow resentful of their parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The principle of equal parental responsibility requires the law to make sure that the cost of recovery of maintenance does not reach unreasonable levels and is not laid on the single parent with custody of the children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There have been cases of mothers who have to drag their children to visit the Courts many times to get their maintenance, as they cannot afford legal representation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many families end up in economic hardship because social service organisations are unable to help as long as the maintenance order is there to be enforced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not a new proposal, as women's organisations have proposed it previously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These powers could include intensive debt collection, investigative surveillance, litigation and overseas travel bans, as in the Australian example.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A central agency, let us call it the Commissioner for the Maintenance of Families, could also serve another purpose, which is to provide support to divorcee families dependent on maintenance so that they would not fall into the poverty trap while waiting for the recovery of owed maintenance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Commissioner for the Maintenance of Families could provide means-tested advance support capped at a quantum to meet basic needs while the owed maintenance is being recovered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My third point concerns maintenance for single unwed parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is in line with the principle of parental responsibility, as the onus of raising children out of wedlock should not fall on the women while men easily avoid taking responsibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is also important for the protection of the children since they are the ones who suffer most and should not be punished for the mistakes of their parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many single unwed mothers, because of their socio-economic background or due to the difficult situation of stigmatisation and isolation they are caught in, are not aware that they could apply for child maintenance from the fathers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Enforcing men's parental responsibility has the knock-on effect of making men responsible in their overall behaviour towards women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My fourth point concerns the tackling of family violence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is there any evidence that the "Many Helping Hands" approach has helped to reduce family violence?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It seems that spousal violence, which makes up the majority of family violence cases, is taking place earlier in the first five years of marriage rather than in the later years of marriage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's approach is to strengthen the touch-points that help identify family violence so that early intervention through counselling can be achieved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is said that the legal route is not the best solution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the Courts and applications for Personal Protection Orders (PPOs) should be the last resort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Notwithstanding this, access to the legal route is an important insurance to give victims a strong sense of security as well as provide an assured deterrence against repeated abuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill restates the persons who can apply for PPOs, which remain severely limited to the very victims of violence or the persons responsible for the victims if they are below the age of 21.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, women and mothers responsible for children being abused are often trapped in precarious positions of recurring violence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Family members, relatives and friends who are explicitly authorised by the victims are in a good position to know when violence takes place and should be empowered to apply for PPOs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Right now, the onus is on the victims to tell doctors about the abuse and request a report for possible PPO application.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By the time the violence results in physical injury, it is at a critical stage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Doctors should be empowered to report cases to the Police and draw up medical reports without request.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In many jurisdictions, mandatory reporting by doctors to law enforcement has helped to mitigate family violence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other than the victims of abuse, children witnessing family violence are the worst affected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most of them would try to intervene and a survey shows 10% called the Police.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to protect the children and tweak the "Many Helping Hands" approach to allow children to become a trip-wire for early intervention.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Allowing incapacitated ex-husbands to claim maintenance from their wives is a belated concession to the principle of gender equality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The call to allow ex-husbands to apply for maintenance was first raised in 1996.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government rejected it on grounds of tradition, that it is the duty of the husband to maintain the wife.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same call was rejected six years ago on account that society is not ready for gender equality when it comes to maintenance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a double irony since the Women's Charter was enacted regardless of whether traditional polygamous society was ready for the modern nuclear family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Gender equality was enshrined in the Charter despite tradition or the readiness of society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Page: 50 Gender equality in 1961 meant giving women equal rights in marriage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, the division of matrimonial assets must be made in "just and equitable" proportions giving due credit to non-financial contributions to marriage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Realising this principle of gender equality today means doing two things.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Men should be given full rights to being eligible for maintenance and we should allow the Courts to make gender-neutral decisions regarding asset division and maintenance based on discernments of financial and non-financial contribution to the matrimonial household and also potential earning power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, the law should factor in opportunity cost in lost earnings due to being a homemaker in the determination of maintenance, especially given that men and women have full access to the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the same spirit of gender equality, but also because this is the hard reality today, we need to include boys and young male persons under Part XI, which protects women and girls from prostitution, sexual exploitation and trafficking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Part is even more outdated than the Women's Charter as it reflects the old colonial Women and Girls' Protection Ordinance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The world in the 21st century has changed and, as scandals regarding the sexual grooming and sexual trafficking of boys indicate, we need to update this Part urgently.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not just for the rationalisation of the law, but it will serve two important purposes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, this Government has reiterated that its ideology and policy are to protect, preserve and promote the modern nuclear family as the bedrock of our society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nowhere else in the law is the modern family so well and morally defined as in the Women's Charter, as equal cooperative partnership with independent rights and parental responsibility has paved the way for families to thrive for 50 years now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is time to rename the Charter to enshrine even more visibly the ideology of safeguarding families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, the renaming does not just give symbolic effect to the moral view of the family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Family Charter will form the basis with which we institutionalise the family further in the era of ageing, globalisation and consumption culture where the norm of non-marital unions and mixed family forms become increasingly prevalent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will be the basis for positive legislation to empower children, men and women to lead healthy family lives if they so desire.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will signal to society that families are here to stay and that the Government is committed to protecting the vulnerable, especially when it comes to our children, to ensure that they do not suffer our failures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Women's Charter is a testament to that spirit, but it is in need of a bold revision that would do justice to its core principles of gender equality and parental responsibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The measures in this Bill try to do this, which is reason for me to support it, but they do not go far enough.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no reason not to be bold.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A bold revision will revive and honour the core principles of the Charter, and this Bill paves the way for the revision.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All that is needed now is the courageous spirit.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It was passed in 1961 to protect and advance the rights of women and girls in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At that time, the typical household division of labour was such that women would take care of the family at home, while men go out to work and bring the bread home.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many women, due to the lack of education and little control over or access to resources then, were often bullied and in worse instances, faced domestic violence.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I believe the Women's Charter passed in 1961 was a progressive and much needed piece of legislation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Fast forward more than 50 years to today, Singapore has progressed significantly and women today have made huge leaps on many fronts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We are capable of holding our own at workplaces.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And with jobs, this means that we are or can be financially independent, generally speaking.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moreover, we have also observed a small, but growing, group of men who give up their jobs to devote full time to caring for their families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, it is timely to review the Women's Charter and update parts of the Charter to offer somewhat more gender balance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For instance, what if the applicant had not even contributed to the raising of the family before he was incapacitated?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These ex-wives may be in financial difficulties themselves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They are also most likely the sole breadwinner supporting their children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She has two young children, two sons still in primary school.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Her husband decided to divorce her for various reasons, but through no fault of hers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She has been working and has been financially independent.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But her financial prowess and position were simply not strong enough for her to afford the payment of the home after the divorce because of the mandatory requirement to sell off the matrimonial flat.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And having custody of her two sons means she will have to take care of them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Yet, despite her being Page: 52 economically active throughout her working life, she was not even able to afford the extra $3,000 to settle the final payment for the home that she was desperately trying to secure in order to continue to provide a stable and normalised life, post-divorce.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, in the likes of Mdm Foo, in the event that her ex-husband happens to be incapacitated and would like to demand for maintenance from her, how would she be able to afford?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This would no doubt impose too much a burden on the likes of Mdm Foo and, in turn, would also impose a great burden and stress, to the disadvantage to the young children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thirdly, what about the divorced women today who are still not receiving their monthly maintenance?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Otherwise, while we may have moved a step forward on the gender equality front, we risk regressing a step backward in terms of protecting vulnerable women – the very group of people this Charter was enacted to protect in the 1960s.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must recognise and support the group of women who had sacrificed the prime of their lives to care for their families and raise their children and, as a result, left themselves in a very vulnerable position.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is made worse-off if they have to also take on the role of being a breadwinner to support their children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I say this because I have a resident whom I feel very sympathetic towards.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I understand the controversy, issues and concerns that the general society may have towards unwed parents, but, in this case, I have full sympathy towards this resident who is just a young lady.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When she was much younger, she met a man who impregnated her and they had three children together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Every time she got pregnant, the man would promise to marry her, but every time, that promise never gets realised.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This poor lady had to fend for herself and to take care of her three children whom she loves dearly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thankfully, her own family is supportive but they, too, are in financial difficulties.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They came to me in tears because they were very upset that this man is going to leave her in the lurch while he marries this other woman whom he felt more attracted to, or for whatever reasons, he felt more strongly about.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The three children will now have to face the consequences and the fate of having to depend on only a single source of resources and, that is, the mother.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This mother is really struggling on her own.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In such instances, I feel very sorry for the three children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is unfair and, therefore, I would like to ask whether MSF can do something to make a provision such that, in such instances, the demand for maintenance from the very irresponsible parent will be made available to the single unwed parent who has to take care of the children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this case, the focus is really on the welfare of the children; they are innocent and they, too, deserve to have an equal and good start in life because they, too, are born Singaporeans and they are the children of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Any end to a marriage can inflict great pain on both the man and woman who once loved each other and chose to be together till death do they part.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, if they have a family, the greatest pain is perhaps borne by their children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Children are born to their parents; they rely on, grow to love and share a deep bond with their parents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But besides targeting divorcing and divorced parents, are there efforts to enhance support for the children affected?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Also, MPP is only for parties who cannot agree on the divorce or ancillary matters.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What about divorcing couples who can agree on all matters?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Their children will still be affected by their parents' separation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On a related note, I believe that ensuring the children have continued access to both parents is important to their development.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, in some acrimonious divorces, the custodian parent may find ways to disallow the other party's access to the children, despite the agreement made.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In some cases, the custodian parent hovers around and makes it difficult for the visiting parent to spend quality time with the children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In some cases, the custodian parent and visiting parent continue to fight during the visitation period.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And in some cases, the custodian parent simply hides the children and refuses to reveal their whereabouts to the visiting parent.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is another example that I came across at the Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS).

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The poor mother came crying to me because she could not have access to her two children as the father decided to smuggle the children out of Singapore to Malaysia.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Since it is out of our jurisdiction in Singapore and she has no relatives or contacts there, she was at a total loss, not knowing where to find her children, but yet she misses them and wanted to make sure they are okay.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This, no doubt, will only worsen the already detrimental impact on the children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Currently, I am glad to note that some voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) have taken the initiative to address this issue.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thye Hua Kwan, for example, has a Centre for Family Harmony at Circuit Road in MacPherson.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I have visited the centre and have also come to understand the plights of some of these divorced parents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This centre allows supervised visitations so that, despite a divorce, both parents can continue to be present and be a responsible father or mother to the child.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As I have said earlier, the biggest victim in a divorce would be the children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Not only do they have to cope with the immediate pain and anxieties, instability and other adjustment issues, they also risk suffering longer-term effects, such as trust and relationship problems in their adulthood.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we must not subject innocent children to such pain as far as possible.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is another group, another category of Singaporean families, that I feel we must continue to support as well – families with foreign parents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In most cases, there are genuine marriages involving a foreign spouse.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Love cannot be ordained; nobody should tell us who we can or cannot marry.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I believe that supporting a family in which most are Singaporeans, that means perhaps with a foreign parent, we are no doubt helping to build strong Singaporean families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I hope that MSF will continue its work in anchoring the ideal of strong families and work closely with other Ministries to ensure that our policies help young couples to build strong Page: 54 families that can stand the test of time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some things the Government cannot and should not interfere, but some things the Government can do to try to facilitate and help.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This, set against the background where the demand for childcare is increasingly high, I believe, is important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is just an example, but I hope that MSF can continue to work with the various agencies and Ministries to look at how we can better support and help our young Singaporean families take root in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the end of the day, the foundation of a strong Singaporean society would be to continue to have strong families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, helping them would, no doubt, help to build a stronger Singapore for the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I support the proposed amendments to the Act.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: "This Bill is making a very great change in the personal lives of the greater majority of our citizens.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It marks a complete break from the past and it is a big step forward.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And it is just for that reason that we have thought it important that we consider this piece of legislation as something outside the ordinary stream of legislation that we consider it to be, in the real sense of the word, a Charter for the women of our State." Mdm Speaker, these words were spoken in earnest by our first Labour and Law Minister Mr K M Byrne during the Second Reading of the Women's Charter Bill on 6 April 1960.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Bill was the culmination of the People's Action Party's (PAP's) rallying call in the 1959 Five Year Plan – "The Tasks Forward".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To give a sense of how important a subject it was, the Five Year Plan dedicated an entire chapter called "Women in the New Singapore".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We last made amendments to the Women's Charter in 2011 to enforce maintenance in divorce cases.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But now, after five years, more amendments are needed to finetune the Women's Charter, in view of the evolving needs of women and children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This Bill has seen numerous and seismic amendments, a sure sign of the importance of the Bill and the difference it has made in society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I will go through them one by one.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A broken home does no wonders to a child's self-confidence, esteem, educational development and health, and many studies attest to this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Divorce is a battle of attrition, as MSF has rightly pointed out.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Children are the losers as they bear the brunt of the collateral damage in any fight between father and mother.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not fair to the Page: 55 children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some may be more resilient and march on bravely in the face of a newly radicalised family environment, but there are many more out there who are left broken, bitter, by divorce.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In many of the cases I have seen at MPS and in block visits, and I am sure many Members can attest to this, it is the children who need the most help.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the years in various Parliamentary Questions, the Ministry of Community Development, Youth and Sports (MCYS) and subsequently MSF, has provided various statistics on children affected by divorce.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Back then, 4,700 and 2,600 for marriages under the Women's Charter and the Administration of Muslim Law Act respectively, and the figures for 2014 have gone up even further.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One can only imagine the fate of the child pre- and post-divorce.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The mental and physical nature of the fights, the ensuing loneliness, and ultimately, the feeling of abandonment would have the child traumatised.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: According to a noted psychologist and researcher, Dr Judith S Wallerstein, who carried out studies on the effects of divorce on the children over a 25-year period, "Divorce is a life-transforming experience.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Adulthood – with the decision to marry, to have or not have children – is different.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Whether the outcome is good or bad, the whole trajectory of an individual's life is profoundly altered by the divorce experience".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The MPP under section 94A is a welcome move.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Through MPP, one can only hope that the child's physical and mental needs are taken care of by both parents.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The programme would be more fruitful if feuding parents could patch up after these counselling sessions, which should be introduced to those considering divorce.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is encouraging that the mandatory programme at CFRC has been quite successful in helping divorcing couples focus on the best interests of their children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Family Justice Courts' CFRC programme has been extended to cover all divorce cases with children below 21 years of age.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I would like to suggest and urge the Ministry to consider pushing this even further: to take a bold move which matches the historic impact of the Women's Charter and, that is, to move this MPP upstream, together with the Mandatory Marriage Preparation programme.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Before I got married to my wife, we needed to attend a compulsory marriage preparation course called Engaged Encounter.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Though it was just one weekend, it was intense and emotional.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It made us realise that courtship and marriage are two very different kettles of fish.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With the support of counsellors and experienced couples who journeyed with us, all of us "junior" couples had the opportunity to ask each other questions that would be too unromantic for courtship but all the more important for a life to be spent together.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To be truthful, through the many marriage preparation courses that are available out there, there are couples who spilt up after attending the courses, but I feel this is for the better.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hasten to add that many of those whom I know have remained friends with one another.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Page: 56 With that in mind, I, therefore, strongly believe that just as courtship does not prepare us for marriage, a wedding does not prepare us for parenthood.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, a mandatory course will equip couples with the ability to stay together and raise a happy family together.
