speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On maintenance for incapacitated men, I feel this is an important step.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I hope that, at some point, we reach parity beyond just providing for those who are incapacitated.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As many Members before me have pointed out, it is not just for parity's sake but it also points to the fact that women in society have improved their social standing by leaps and bounds and this must be applauded.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The late Mr Lee Kuan Yew, at his 1983 National Day Rally, mentioned that our economy is dependent on women and their contributions to Singapore and this is invaluable.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He said: "We've got to go one step beyond and try and fit in the problems in a new context.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In other words, how do we so reshape our policies that we can educate them; that they will have full career opportunities that the valuable well-educated, whilst making a big contribution, will, at the same time, ensure their contribution to the next generation?" The generation that Mr Lee referred to so stirringly in that speech made more than 30 years ago, is this generation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Since then, women in Singapore have been breaking, in fact, smashing the glass ceiling.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Before this amendment, there was mutual obligation under the Charter but not when deciding maintenance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This amendment will also put an end to the dysfunctional carryover from common law that will fully restore equality to women in marriage.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Although such an amendment to the Women's charter was not considered in 1996 nor subsequently in 2011, this is an important first step.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I, however, hope that, at some point, we reach parity beyond just, as I mentioned, providing for those who are incapacitated.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What are the parameters as well, as alluded to by the hon Member Ms Tin Pei Ling, to determine the level of incapacity and how will ex-husbands be deemed to be fully incapacitated?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hope the Ministry would shed more light on this area.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: An upgrade from the proposed single MRO under the set of amendments, as mentioned by the Minister earlier, is a suggestion to set up a formal Tribunal, akin to the Tribunal for the Maintenance of Parents, to free the Courts and to determine and enforce maintenance payments for both ex-husbands and ex-wives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The late Mdm Chan Choy Siong advocated for Marriage Counselling Courts in 1959 and this came to fruition only in 1995 with the setting up of the Family Justice Courts.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hope that while maintenance for husbands took 19 years and the Family Court took 36 years to find realisation, it will not take another similar length of time before a tribunal is Page: 57 considered.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These findings, of course, showed that over one-third of victimised women, or 35.8%, received some injuries during the most recent incidents.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe that, for some, their ordeal does not end there.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Minister, in his proposed amendment, has indicated that, in certain circumstances, women and children can be placed in the care of a fit personnel.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But in cases like these where they are not placed in places of safety, such as a residential care home or a crisis centre, will their safety be compromised, because they do not have a proper set up for security measures?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These places of safety are supposed to offer a sanctuary to abused women and girls.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And if this sanctuary fails to provide the promised protection, we will be deemed to have failed in our duty.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With regard to voiding marriages of convenience, it is timely that deterrent action has been taken to reign in the number of sham marriages.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: ICA has mentioned that the women in some of these marriages are sex workers or are made to prostitute themselves after the so-called legalities of the sham marriage.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Under the amendment proposed in this Bill, would a statutory declaration be enough to further deter such sham marriages?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Women form the core of a family and are the pillars of strength of society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They have contributed much and will contribute even more, as the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew has stated.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the words of Mdm Chan Choy Siong, in her opening remarks on the debate on the Women's Charter, "  will bring about revolutionary change in society." I believe that this Charter will continue to be revolutionary, and all the more so with these amendments.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would not call them belated, but perhaps a timely evolution.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While we take small steps with each amendment, women have taken giant leaps forward and, therefore, in this context, Page: 58 Mdm Speaker, I support this Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In my practice, I have assisted many clients in their divorce proceedings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One of the issues that is usually very difficult for couples to deal with is the arrangements in relation to the custody, care and control of and access to the children upon divorce.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have often heard stories of how the children become embroiled in their parents' acrimonious battles in Court and become emotional pawns in the situation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Minister earlier alluded to this with some examples.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have also encountered first-hand parties who let their children read their affidavits and those of their soon-to-be former spouse on the pre-text that the children should know what is happening.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Or those who make their children write notes or letters to Court to say that they do not want to be with the other parent.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In my view, such actions are harmful to the children's mental development in the long run.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The negativity which the parents show towards each other can have a traumatic impact on the children and usually, these children are unable to voice out their emotions to the parents.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I recall a Family Court Judge sharing in one of the lectures I attended some years back.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As adults, when we are unhappy or stressed, most of us can reach out for help, talk about our emotions with our family and friends.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, children may not be able to articulate their emotions as well and may not even have the opportunities to do so.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, the divorce process should be child-centric and protect the interests of the children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would often advise my clients to try to put aside their grievances when it comes to matters relating to their children and always give paramount interest and consideration to their children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For the parents, this is actually easier said than done.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have come to realise that, most times, parties are too caught up with their emotions to be able to think rationally in the situation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They are angry, hurt and, sometimes even vengeful.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is important to put them in the right state of mind before they begin their divorce proceedings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Over the years, there have been many developments at the Family Court to gradually introduce mandatory counselling and mediation for parties with young children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think it is useful to clarify the intent of excluding certain groups from MPP, especially if we want to ensure that as many parents as possible are educated about the impact of Page: 59 divorce on their children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The intent of introducing an MPP is clearly noble.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, for the initiative to be truly successful, MPP itself must be effective.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In implementing this programme, I hope attention will be given to develop a curriculum that goes to the core of the problem and is going to be useful for the parents.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Such programmes should address the parents' needs, cater to the various family situations and be simple enough to be understood by all.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In fact, the Minister mentioned that there were concerns raised during the public consultation exercise.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If there are insufficient slots, for example, parties would have to wait before they can attend the programme and they may be delayed in filing their divorce papers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This can cause angst and frustration amongst the already stressed and highly emotional couples.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Divorce is an agonising process and we should not delay or complicate the procedures unnecessarily.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In keeping with making the divorce process more child-centric, I also welcome and appreciate the proposed amendments to section 50 of the Women's Charter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Where children are involved, whether they like it or not, couples will continue to be in a long-term relationship.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: An adversarial Court process can be damaging to parties and, in particular, their children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is, therefore, important to have processes that in some way "heal" parties, to help them cope with the situation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that counselling and mediation are key "healing" processes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is useful to extend the variety of such processes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that section 50 also extends to all proceedings under the Women's Charter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These involve disputes between families, between spouses or former spouses, between siblings and between parent and child.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Family Court has, over time, taken a lot of effort in developing many aspects of the Family Justice System, including having mediators specially trained in family mediation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need to continue building the family justice ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In particular, for divorce, we need to continue on the existing efforts of developing specialised lawyers who are equipped with appropriate knowledge and skills to handle divorces and other family disputes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Specialised lawyers can promote collaborative divorce, which encourages parties to discuss and resolve their disputes amicably.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: When parties can resolve matters on their own and avoid litigation, there is a greater chance that the relationship can remain cordial and their children are spared from the acrimony.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I personally have some concerns about the call for allowing husbands in general, or former husbands, to claim maintenance from their wives.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Yes, as a divorce lawyer, I also have male clients, and some have indicated unhappiness with the current regime in the Women's Charter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I Page: 60 acknowledge that while many Singaporean women have made good progress, this has not been uniform across all groups of women.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: While the Ministry takes steps to keep pace with societal changes, I believe there is a need to recognise that the majority of women still lag behind their male counterparts, especially financially.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A wife is more likely to have given up her career or job advancement to care for the family.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Very often, we still see the traditional dynamics of the woman being the principal caregiver to her children, even when both husband and wife are working.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Currently, I believe there is still some way to go in developing parity of financial status between men and women, especially across various income levels.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The developments in the law, while they should be robust, need to be relevant and reflect the current state of affairs in society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am of the view that it is lofty to think that we should advocate gender equality without testing it against the actual realities of the society today.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Women's Charter was enacted in 1961 with the intent to protect and advance the rights of women and girls in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It included regulations on the relationship between husband and wife, the relationship between parents and their children, termination of marriages, division of matrimonial assets and maintenance.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Women's Charter also provides protection against family violence and the penalty for offences against women and girls.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Several amendments have been made since 1961, with the latest amendment made in 2011 to strengthen the enforcement of maintenance orders, provide improved support to those affected by divorces, as well as address emerging trends in marriages and divorce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The changes to the Women Charter, as proposed in the Bill tabled for today's Reading are positive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They are up to date and take into account the changing realities in the family in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Like many who have spoken before me, I think this is a very important step as it does take the interest of the child who is involved in the divorce, at the centre.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Minister has shared that much of the content of this programme is around the care of the child, housing and schools, which are very important.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I do want to ask for more elaboration on the duration of MPP.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The amendment also indicates that the person appointed to conduct MPP will determine whether any person that attends the programme has completed the programme.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Although an appeal against the determination can be made to the Page: 61 Minister, what measures will be put in place to ensure that the primary objective of protecting the interest of the children involved is met and that the case can be resolved effectively?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I feel that this amendment is fair as it recognises the support expected of husband and wife during times of illness and disability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is in line with the spirit of the Women's Charter, as outlined in the Rights and Duties of Husband and Wife in Part VI, clause 46, where it says that "Upon the solemnisation of marriage, the husband and the wife shall be mutually bound to co-operate with each other in safeguarding the interests of the union and in caring and providing for the children." I have personally seen several cases during my MPS where wives have left their husbands after they were diagnosed with serious illnesses like cancer and they were left with no means to support themselves.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This amendment, however, does assume that the wife has an income and the means to be able to afford the maintenance.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This may or may not always be the case.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And as the wife will most likely need to provide for the children as the husband is incapacitated, this may also put a heavy financial strain on her, even if she is working.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must also recognise that many women do make career choices to either slow down their careers or even leave their jobs for some period of time, if not permanently, when they have young children.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This does disrupt their career, re-entry into the workforce, as well as their income.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Court, in deciding whether to order the wife to provide maintenance for her husband, I hope will take into account her financial circumstances and the need to provide for herself and her children.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Regarding protection for women, girls and residents at places of safety, and professionals engaged in protection work, while all of us are talking about the progress that we see in Singapore, I think the Bill recognises the need for protection of vulnerable women and girls.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The sad reality is that they need protection as their abusers are usually their family members.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The study also discovered that while victims of spousal abuse came from all age groups, the majority are females in their 30s and 40s.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The study also found that spousal victims and abusers were better educated.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As the abusers in these cases are men, they will be, in all probability, considerably physically stronger than them, and, as they are family, they will have also emotional control over the women.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Thus, a shelter or safe place which provides for their requisite safety is imperative for them, not just to ensure that they are physically safe, but that they are also given peace of mind to pick up the pieces so that they can continue with their lives.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They need reassurance that their abusers will not be able to locate them when they are having sanctuary in shelters.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Straits Times news article by Janice Tai published in November 2013 on the study also helped to give some insight into the rise of family violence.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I quote: "The worsening problem of family violence can be seen by the rise in the number of such cases that went to Court.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In 1995, the Family Court heard 978 such cases.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will prevent perpetrators of violence from harassing, intimidating or harming the persons residing and working at these places.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This amendment does provide for the state to also take action against serious breaches that would compromise the safety of residents and staff.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There has been much discussion today around the question, "Do we still need the Women's Charter?" When the Women's Charter was passed in 1961, the intent was to protect the rights of women.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must recognise that, since then, there has been much progress made in Singapore and we have seen strong advancement of women from education to their participation in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Some may then argue that there is not a need for the Women's Charter or that this is discriminating against men.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I agree that there has, indeed, been great progress in the advancement of women in Singapore in education, health, employment and income.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, there are still several areas that women lag behind men.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many of our hon Members have touched on this, and this includes salary, labour force participation, especially in the economically productive years, in senior management, and decision-making roles in organisations, including boards.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While we are all seeing a trend in Singapore of men increasingly playing a bigger role in the family and involvement in caregiving, in the majority of households, women still play the primary caregiver role.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In Singapore, there are almost the same numbers of men and women attending university and obtaining degrees.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But we still, however, see many women leaving the workforce to take care of their children and family members.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are still fewer women in senior leadership roles in organisations compared to men.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But if we actually look at the labour force participation of women aged 25 to 39, this has dropped significantly, compared to the total number of women and single women in labour force participation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, it is likely that these women left their work during the prime years of their career to take care of their children and family.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are also seeing greater participation of husbands in the home, as I have shared earlier, and some have even chosen to be the stay-at-home parent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, while this trend will likely increase, for now, women continue to take on a greater role and family caring responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Women's Charter is more than just about the relationship between husband and wife and that of between parents and their children, and the division of matrimonial assets when marriages fail.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are still vulnerable groups of women and girls who need protection.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I believe that there is continued relevance of the Women's Charter in Singapore today.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The last time this Bill was debated in January 2011, I also spoke it.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Then, amongst other things, I was asking for men to be given reasonable access to their children by their ex-wives.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I believe the numbers to be small, though the Ministry does not reveal the figures of those who may be impacted.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Moreover, the Court will still take into consideration the financial ability of the woman first before deciding if her ex-spouse is legally entitled to maintenance from his wife.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think this is the right thing to do.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I am mindful that it is still mostly women and their children who need help to recover maintenance/alimony fees from their ex-husbands.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Hence, the critics of this Bill who say that we should be more concerned about this larger group rather than the smaller one, I think, missed the point.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, the amendment does not change this level of help.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Second, the group may be small, but their cause is no less just.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Before I proceed, I should declare my interest as a board member of the Centre for Fathering – a non-profit organisation with an Institution of Public Character (IPC) status and a champion for the "Dads for Life" movement.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have been on the board longer than I have been in politics.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is commonplace when we speak of gender equality to think that we speak on behalf of women.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But there is something unusual about male dependants.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I wish to draw Parliament's attention to this unusual group of men – bright men of amiable dispositions and ability, who choose to be homemakers while their wives work.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These husbands and fathers have embraced the role-reversal, because wife and husband believe it works best for their family unit.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Again, this is the minority, and 47,000 or 25% of females aged 25 to 54 cited childcare for their not being in the labour force.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The gap is still there, but it is steadily narrowing over 30 years.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Certainly, nothing wrong nor surprising with these trends.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Second, the economics of home care and paid work follow this reversal.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And when it comes to recompense, men should not be unjustly denied.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But, somehow, in more than 30 years, it has not been able to get through this House.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Back in 2011, it was raised in Parliament that role reversals were increasingly common; the wife takes on the sole breadwinner role and the husband stays behind to take care of the house and family.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If the couple were to divorce, the husband should be allowed to claim maintenance Page: 64 from the woman.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In that year, that is, 2011, in response to calls for gender equality for men to be able to claim maintenance from women, the then-Minister for Community Development, Youth and Sports, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, said, and I quote, "14 years ago, the Select Committee said we were not ready yet.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I am afraid at this point in time, the answer is still we are not ready yet.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I hope it will not take another 14 years but I am sure every time we review the Women's Charter, this question will arise." Mdm Speaker, today, we are into this cycle of 14 years.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, are we finally ready after almost 30 years of debate?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I say, let us recognise the contributions of stay-at-home men and the notion of shared participation between two equals.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This year, we mark the 55th anniversary of the Women's Charter, a piece of legislation made for a time when women needed special protection.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Perhaps in another 55 years, at a time of true equality, we would not need such a charter.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But until then, let us make the law a little more equal, by offering men the same protection as women.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the eyes of the law at least, we all ought to be equal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, I believe that special consideration should be given to cases of domestic violence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand from the Association of Women for Action and Research (AWARE) that their experience is that the abused spouse is usually the one who wants the divorce whereas the abusive spouse may resist.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this situation, since the couple would not have agreed on divorce and all ancillary matters, according to the proposed amendment, they would have to go through MPP unless this is dispensed with by the Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am concerned that the abused spouse could end up being trapped in a legally perpetuated situation of domestic violence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will not be in the interest of the child as, in addition to spousal abuse, there may also be child abuse in such a situation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that spousal maintenance should be based on the principle of fairness, rather than gender.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Maintenance should also be available to men in other appropriate cases, for example, where men make economic sacrifices to Page: 65 take a primary role in household labour and caregiving, even if such cases are rarely encountered.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the moment, section 160 allows the Director of Social Welfare to detain girls aged between16 and 21 on the following grounds: (a) if her lawful guardian requests the Director to detain her; (b) if the Director considers her to be in need of protection and whose lawful guardian cannot be found; (c) if the Director believes her to have been ill-treated; and lastly, (d) if the Director considers her to be in moral danger.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is there any investigation of the "lawful guardian" who makes such a request?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is the girl in question consulted about her own needs or wishes?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The underlying assumption is that the "lawful guardian" always has the girl's best interests at heart; this would not be true in situations of family violence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even if the lawful guardians have their charges' best interests in mind, after the girl has been brought into detention, the Director can detain her until 21 years old, according to the amendment, and the guardian would have no control.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is problematic that girls can be detained against their will when they have not committed any criminal offences and, in fact, are in vulnerable situations at times.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The provisions of sections 160, 161 and 163, even after the amendment, are still overly vague, broad and open-ended.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is still no clear information about the Director of Social Welfare's decision-making process concerning whether or not to bring a girl into detention, how long to detain her and what the conditions of her detention should be.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are the factors and criteria used for decision-making?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that we can have more explicit definitions of the conditions under which minors may be placed in protective shelters, including domestic violence as one of these conditions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also hope that there will be submissions of the decisions of the Director of Social Welfare, with justifications, to the Family Court with a Court review and a Court order required for continuation of protective shelter for the woman or girl at risk, with the duration of the stay stipulated as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the end of the period of stay, the case should be reviewed by the Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On the PPO regime, I note the amendment to section 65 to allow married or previously married persons below the age of 21 to apply for a protection order and expedited order for themselves and specific dependants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is commendable, but it does not follow that a wife under 21 with her dependants can easily find shelter in a place of safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will shelters for victims of domestic violence now accept married girls and women under 21?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If not, what provisions are there for a wife who is under 21 and a victim of domestic violence to be housed in a place of safety?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, I suggest that other than those who are married, all individuals under 21 be allowed to apply for Personal Protection Orders (PPOs) and Domestic Exclusion Orders (DEOs) so that they can be protected from all forms of domestic violence, that the need for parental consent be removed in such cases and that the application for protection can be made against anyone in their household.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I seek more clarity as to the process by which a marriage would be found void under the proposed new section 11A.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 11A(3) makes it clear Page: 66 that marriages will be deemed void if certain immigration offences are committed, but are there other circumstances in which section 11A would be invoked?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, is there a Court process involved or is it just an administrative determination?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In my view, a decision of such gravity should be subject to judicial process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, make spousal maintenance available, regardless of gender, on the basis of fairness and need.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I seek more clarifications on this and also for the submission of the decisions of the Director of Social Welfare under this section to be reviewed by the Family Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Legislation is only one piece of the puzzle.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are also policies, support programmes and services and public education.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are all part of the overall effort.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Families and the community also have a strong role to play in strengthening and supporting families.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Like many Bills and policies, all of us would like more to be done.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Some of us would feel that we could go further, especially on matters, such as maintenance of men, marriages involving minors and enhancing maintenance enforcements for wives, ex-wives and children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: These are options we considered but, as I mentioned, societal attitudes, while changing in the directions which Members have highlighted, are also not uniform.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: From our consultations, it was clear that there were a fair number of Singaporeans who will feel that it would be too fast and too far if we move further at this stage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: On one hand, while some of us may feel that to make some of these important changes represents a bold direction, but I think it is also Page: 67 about being effective, relevant and calibrating the different sensitivities involved because a lot of these issues are, in many ways, emotive.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Legislation is an important part, but it is not everything, because you cannot legislate everything.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: What we plan and intend to do and carry out is to make sure that where there are needs to be met, the needs will have to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It need not be addressed fully necessarily by legislation itself, but programmes, services have to be there.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And especially, as highlighted, family and community play a very important part as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I would also like to highlight that this idea of a Family Charter was something our Ministry has looked at as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is something, as pointed out by Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, that we keep on the table.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have looked at it intently and, as we have mentioned, there are different views on how we should interpret this.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But what I would like to highlight is this: the emphasis on the family remains.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Just because we do not call it a Family Charter does not, in itself, mean that we are not placing emphasis on the family.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: For all intents and purposes, the bulk of what we are setting out in the Women's Charter is aimed at supporting families and, moreover, whilst the Act is so named, its provisions are, in fact, gender-neutral, except in the areas of maintenance – which many Members have raised their views on as well – protection of women and girls, vice, prostitution activities.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In other areas of the law, others are also covered.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: For example, boys are covered under the Prevention of Human Trafficking Act and also under the Children and Young Persons Act (CYPA).

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have noted the points raised and this is something that we will continue to review as time goes by.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The Women's Charter, when it was first launched, was a landmark Charter.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Over the years, important changes have been made.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This time round, important changes are being made as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: While in some areas we are taking calibrated steps forward, society, like I said, is not static.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will continue to monitor how society evolves, continue to consult and continue to look at the suggestions and ideas brought up by many Members.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Alex Yam suggested that these young couples also attend a parenting programme.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Indeed, the mandatory marriage preparation programme covers aspects of parenting.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It also helps the couple to understand how their relationship will evolve when they start a family and have children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: If the bride is expecting, grandparents are also invited to join in as extended family support is critical to the soon-to-be young parents.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Dr Lily Neo would be pleased to know that our enhanced marriage support framework will also help young couples to address challenges during their marriage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This includes link-ups to appropriate parenting programmes and support.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Many Members expressed empathy for children caught in the middle of their parents' divorce.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Dr Lily Neo shared about the negative impact on Page: 68 children and highlighted the need for assistance to ensure that children do not fall through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: My Ministry appointed the Divorce Support Specialist Agencies (DSSAs) to provide a continuum of care to divorced families.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Many of us come into contact with such cases as well, either through friends or the residents we meet.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I think it is important that children remain the centre of our efforts.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Giving voice to children comes in many ways but we need to be careful because, as we all know, sometimes, in an acrimonious divorce process, children become part of the game.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They are being pitted, back and forth, between the couples.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That can be very disturbing and can have a tremendous impact on the children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: What we want to make sure is that throughout the whole process, the children's interests are looked after.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We want to make sure that they can undergo individual counselling.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They may also attend an evidence-based programme called "Children-In-Between", which equips children with the skills to manage their feelings and develop resilience.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Parents are also asked to attend, so that they reinforce the skills learnt by their children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Some of the stories I shared were very much surfaced through some of these processes where the children are encouraged to speak up so they could articulate their concerns and the things that trouble them.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But that is not something that we take for granted; it is something that we need to continue to work on.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ms Jessica Tan asked for some details of the divorce support programmes.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I will just very quickly run through how we are approaching it.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: There are also counselling made available to rebuild the marriage and, as mentioned earlier, the "Children-in-Between" programme.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: There is also a Parenting PACT, which is a consultation session for divorced parents with minor children, designed to help parents understand the impact of a divorce on their children, learn co-parenting strategies and so on.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: There is a whole range of support being brought to bear, before filing for divorce, during the whole process itself and thereafter.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will be quite happy to explore other measures that we can put in place to support families in this process.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Louis Ng suggested that the MPP should be automatically waived for victims of family violence in order to expedite the divorce proceedings and highlighted the particular profile of the families undergoing these difficulties.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I think there is an even greater need for these divorcing parties to be directed to receive help.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have measures in place to minimise the risk to victims of abuse.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The idea is that while we do recognise the challenges that families face when violence occurs, we also recognise that these families need help and to intervene where we can.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We also make sure that clauses are available, steps are available for families to be assisted even when this violence is perpetuated and continues to be perpetuated.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Another area that garnered much interest was spousal maintenance.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Members have put forth a wide spectrum of views.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Members, such as Mr Seah Kian Peng, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh and Mr Louis Ng, spoke about moving towards a more gender-neutral approach.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I fully understand because we do see instances where there might seem to be a compelling need to move along these grounds while, on the other hand, as I have highlighted, there are also other views.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam expressed her concerns against it, reminding us that many women are still vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I also heard concerns about extending maintenance to incapacitated husbands, such as those shared by Ms Tin Pei Ling.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The scenario of a woman of lesser means struggling to support herself and the children is a big concern.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: What more if such a woman had to maintain her incapacitated ex-husband.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: To reiterate, the incapacitated husband must meet all the criteria set out before he can apply for maintenance from the wife.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Even if all these criteria are met, it does not mean that the husband or ex-husband will automatically be entitled to maintenance.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Dr Lily Neo expressed concerns for women who may be caught up in these situations where it will be a strain for them to provide maintenance for incapacitated husbands as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: So, the Court will have to consider all circumstances of the case, including the income and earning capacity of the wife or ex-wife, the financial needs of both parties and the needs of the children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is no different from the considerations for maintenance for wives and ex-wives, where they are also not automatically entitled to maintenance, as highlighted by some of the examples that we have mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It strikes a balance at this stage of our societal development.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As rightly pointed out by Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Ms Sun Xueling, there must be a clear priority to better enforce maintenance payments and to improve the process.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And, indeed, I fully agree with many Members who have cited many examples that they have come across.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The purpose of this officer is to assist Page: 70 the Courts to better assess if a defaulter is incorrigible and, therefore, allows the Courts to take firm action against him, if it is so.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will also constantly and continually explore how to improve the processes and to make it less onerous for all those affected.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is something we recognise and we work closely with the Family Justice Courts on this as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: All couples marrying under the Women's Charter must undergo document verification and make a statutory declaration on matters relating to the intended marriage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Where there are doubts, the Registry of Marriages (ROM) staff will interview the couple separately and explain the consequences of entering into a marriage of convenience.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have found this useful, intervening at this stage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Also, the Registrar will not issue any marriage licence to the couple unless the Registrar is satisfied that the intended marriage meets the conditions under the Women's Charter.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if the decision to void a marriage should be subjected to the judicial process.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Such cases would have been scrutinised through the judicial process.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is only consistent that such marriages are consequentially and automatically void, given that the act of entering into such a marriage is an offence.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Louis Ng suggested that all persons under 21 years be allowed to apply for a PPO and DEO for themselves against anyone in their household, without the need for parental consent.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It would be in a minor's interests to have a reliable adult apply on their behalf.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The application may be made by the parent who is not the perpetrator of violence.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: If the parents or guardians are themselves the violence perpetrators, a relative or any social worker appointed by the Minister, can step in, without the need for consent from the minor's parents or guardians.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked about the circumstances in which the Director of Social Welfare can detain vulnerable female minors aged 16 to 21 in places of safety.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: All cases which come to the attention of the Director are thoroughly investigated.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked if married minors who have suffered domestic violence can seek refuge at places of safety.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Yes, they can seek accommodation and support from crisis shelters.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Alex Yam asked about incidents where the security of places of safety was compromised and measures to protect the residents and professionals.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In both instances, the Police took swift action as the shelters had established good networks with them.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: No one was hurt in both incidents but I do take on-board the Member's concerns.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The Women's Charter is a piece of legislation with historical significance that seeks to balance the interests of different groups – the rights and protection of spouses, ex-spouses and their Page: 71 children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Members such as Ms Jessica Tan have also reaffirmed its relevance.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will work closely with stakeholders as well as this House to shape our legislation to better reflect the changing Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: At the same time, notwithstanding legislation, we will make sure that there are programmes in place to support Singaporeans who do have need for help.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: At the same time, I encourage families and the community to play an active role to support families in need.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Our efforts obviously must not end with the legislative changes.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We all have a collective responsibility to support good marriages and positive parent-child relationships.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Strong families are indeed a haven for each and every child.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Alex Yam, please keep your clarification short.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: I note the Minister's point on the mandatory parenting component for minor couples.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Will the Minister consider extending both programmes for all couples before marriage and not just minor couples?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: The second clarification is on the Tribunal for Maintenance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Will the said Tribunal be considered by the Ministry in the near future?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Lastly, I thank the Minister for the clarification on safety at crisis shelters.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: But how will this be ensured for those who are under the care of fit persons who do not have the benefit of security measures or closed circuit television?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: The second clarification is on whether a Tribunal for Maintenance will be considered by the Ministry in the near future.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We believe that there are counselling, programmes and support made available for all couples who are seeking help or who are looking for support.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is very much the responsibility of parents to see through their responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As we all know, there are those who fail to do it.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I want to highlight again, it is important to remember, that while we encounter frustrating cases where individuals do not receive their maintenance, there are two scenarios.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: One, there are fathers who are not able to pay because of the circumstances in which they find themselves.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And it is important for us to understand and to check to fully understand the background and extend the appropriate assistance.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Page: 72 The latter group, which I have less sympathy for, are those who can pay but refuse to pay.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Setting up a tribunal is one approach but actually the laws are in place.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will run all the necessary checks, so that we will try to minimise the burden on the women who are affected and then having the law to come in.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That should have a salutary effect on those concerned.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will continue to keep a watch on this because we recognise that it is frustrating and difficult for the women involved and their families.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As for the safety of crisis shelters, we hear the Member's perspectives.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: For those we feel are particularly vulnerable, we would place them in crisis shelters.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We also conduct checks in terms of those families and other safe places where we put the children in.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Basically, what we have is a graduated approach to security.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: For those who need a much more secure environment, we will make sure that crisis shelters are available for them.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: For the others, we have a slightly more step-down provision.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In fact, if we extend it further, there will be vulnerable children in other scenarios as well whom we should think about tracking.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is something that I have discussed with my colleagues in MSF, especially for troubled youths who have fallen afoul of the law, who have encountered problems, and whether we should track them and subsequently when they are looking at settling down, for example, do we also provide them counselling support and so on.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As Members would realise, with the numbers of divorces taking place and children being affected, to maintain a register of the affected children and to track them over the years, it is quite a heavy responsibility.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We do not plan to do this at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: What we do want to make sure is that the support programmes are in place, whether by divorce or other circumstances.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That means that for those who need help and support, counselling, support programmes, are available, so that they can provide both the children and the families support and for them to come forward to seek it when there is a need.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: To track them and to ensure that they are constantly being provided this support, that is a very different order of magnitude.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: At this point in time, we are not looking at that, but I take the Member's suggestion on-board.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: While we encourage individuals to come forward, we also encourage family members to bring them forward for these support programmes, should there be a need.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can I ask the Minister for a clarification with regard to section 160?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Is it solely the Director of Social Welfare who makes a decision to detain a girl or is it up to a team of people?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If it is solely up to one person, then may I ask if we could have a proposed amendment to make it a team of people that makes this decision?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Because in other jurisdictions, when the Police are able to apply for protection orders, it does have a salutary effect on the perpetrators in reducing family violence, especially when it is coupled with early intervention, such as counselling and what not.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That is why we want to make sure that help is available for the concerned minor and that other adults can be brought to bear.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Our Ministry can also direct individuals to support them.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Where family violence is involved, it can be very emotive.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Where a family member is the perpetrator, we want to make sure that other parties are able to advise and help them make the application.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I would just like to qualify that, earlier on, what I said was a register more for vulnerable children, and I did not really say for all children of divorces.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: So, would the Minister at least consider identifying such children, disadvantaged children, and then keep them on MSF’s radar, so that we can give them assistance on a long-term basis?

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Like I said, the key thing is to make sure that the support programmes are in place, that assistance can be provided to children who are affected and for them or their families to come forward.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We do recognise that vulnerable individuals, especially when they are young, do have serious concerns and whether we should play a much more active role on that front.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That is something that we are looking at.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I have a question: would the MRO have any enforcement ability?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I read that the role of the MRO is to obtain information on parties' financial circumstances to assist the Court in its fact-finding process and also have a standing in Court to tender the information obtained.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, is the ultimate penalty still a warrant of arrest on the defaulter?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Who, then, enforces this warrant of Page: 74 arrest?

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: If they are deemed to be able to pay and not actively paying their maintenance, that is when the Courts will enforce some of these measures.      .

text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair again at 4.35 pm.
